messages.subject: Important ISEC dates and information
messages.subject_clean: Important ISEC dates and information
messages.body_plain:
Hello friends and colleagues (and apologies for cross posting!),

Here is some information and important dates as we creep closer to ISEC24. The links and information for the items below will start appearing on the new ISEC website over the next two weeks (https://statisticalecology.org/, the dedicated website for ISEC conferences from now on).

Please share this information with your friends, colleagues, and students.

Looking forward to seeing you all in Swansea in the summer

Luca and the ISEC organising committee.

ISEC2024: The International Statistical Ecology Conference

15th – 19th July 2024

Swansea, UK

Keynote Speaker

We are excited to announce that we have confirmed a fantastic collection of keynote speakers for the conference this year (details on the website):

Dr. Marie Auger-Méthé (University of British Columbia, Canada)
Prof. John Fieberg (University of Minnesota, USA)
Prof. Rachel McCrea (Lancaster University, UK)
Dr. Matthew Schofield (University of Otago, NZ)
Dr. Elise Zipkin (Michigan State University, USA)

Registration and accommodation

Registration will open in the next 2 weeks with a registration deadline of 15th June. There will be a ‘standard delegate rate’ and a (reduced) ‘student delegate rate’ and the costs will be in line with previous rates. There will be no ‘early bird’ rate.  We have arranged a block booking for on-site university accommodation. These rooms will be held until the end of April, which is after decisions will be announced about abstracts (see below). This accommodation is, of course, optional.

Abstract submission

Abstract submission will open in the next 2 weeks and will close on Friday 22nd of March. Abstract will be submitted vias the website (link to appear soon). Decisions about abstracts will be communicated by early April. There will be standard talks and posters.

Workshops

We are now welcoming proposals for workshops! If you are interested in proposing a workshop, please send the following information to Luca Borger (l.borger [at] swansea.ac.uk <http://swansea.ac.uk>) and Chris Sutherland (css6 [at] st-andrews.ac.uk <http://st-andrews.ac.uk>):
Title
Short workshop description (<300 word)
Intended audience
Whether you are proposing a ½ day or a full day workshop
We will charge a small fee for workshops which will be used to cover the registration of workshop instructors and refreshments.

Chris

While I may be sending this email outside of my normal office hours, I have no expectation to receive a reply outside of yours.

Chris Sutherland (he/him/his)

Reader

Centre for Research into Ecological & Environmental Modelling

School of Mathematics and Statistics
University of St Andrews

W: website <https://www.sutherlandecology.com/>

E: cs...@st-andrews.ac.uk

messages.subject: Large scale simulations of lynx
messages.subject_clean: Large scale simulations of lynx
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently running simulations for an entire Eurasian lynx population in Central Europe that includes resident and dispersing individuals, the latter of which are about 25% of the total count.

As dispersing individuals have lower g0s and higher sigmas, I'm curious if it is more correct to model them as a separate population with different parameters, as is shown at the end of the secrdesign vignette for group simulations with males and females.

However, perhaps this separate approach is not necessary, as the dispersing individuals would have a lower weight in the results compared to the more abundant residents. For example, Ash et al. (2020) did not distinguish the groups when they simulated tigers.

Thank you very much,
Stefano Palmero

messages.subject: Question about suitable buffer width
messages.subject_clean: Question about suitable buffer width
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been analysing some camera trapping data using secr for the first time, with a mark-resight model, and am unsure about my choice of buffer. I understand that the density should reach an asymptote with increasing buffer width, and by running the model multiple times with different buffer widths, I can see this happening. However, the density only levels out at around 8km, which seems way too large for what we know about the home ranges/movements of these animals. I'd expect a sensible buffer to be about 4km.

I tried comparing the hazard function vs. half-normal but these gave similar results. I am not sure what to try next, or whether to leave the buffer at 4km or 8km. Any ideas would be welcome. I'm new to this type of analysis so this might be a simple issue!

Many thanks,

Erica

Dear Murray,

I'm still new to secr and was playing around a bit. I assumed R crashing was a result of my inadequate usage of the secr.fit function. However, when coming across this conversation, I thought it might be worth flagging that bug.

I have a very similar set up with a polygon detector and came across a similar or likely even the same error:
running secr.fit with groups instead of hcov, e.g. model=g0~g, groups = "mycovariate" and/or the option to specify the covariate via model = g0~mycovariate (instead of hcov) causes R to crash.

I'm using secr 4.6.4 and sex (f, m) as my covariate. The hcov approach mentioned above runs without crashing, and when discretizing the polygon (as suggested to Henriette) the groups argument works too.

If I understand correctly, you generally recommend discretizing polygon detectors, since analysis run faster and are more robust despite being less "accurate" (for lack of better word) due to artifacts introduced from the discretization?

Many thanks,
Lukas

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Murray! Also, for pointing out that lambda0 (and not g0) is the appropriate detection parameter for polygon detectors (since they use hazard functions).

My previous message was a bit unclear, apologies. As mentioned, my covariate is sex (two levels: f, m; no NAs). While D~Sex works, both using sigma~Sex and (the wrong use of) g0~Sex cause R to crash. Both instances were set to CL = TRUE. The suggested use of lambda0~Sex with CL=TRUE also causes a fatal error.
Regarding the use of groups=”Sex”, I'd set CL=FALSE. Here, R crashes as well both when specifying the model with D~g; sigma~g; or lambda0~g respectively.

I’m interested in estimating densities. I expect sex differences in density as well as home range sizes, further I also suspect differences in detection.
While I went through vignettes, pdfs and conversations in this group, I’m still not sure if I understood everything correctly. Apart from modelling separate female and male sessions, there are three options for modelling the sex differences:
Sex as group, i.e. groups=”Sex” & model term with ~g
Sex as an individual covariate, i.e. model term with ~Sex
In the case of Sex, the individual covariate corresponds to two discrete groups, thus no preference in which approach to choose? While the group (full likelihood) models use density as a model parameter, the individual covariate (conditional likelihood) models derive density. Does that mean that in I my case, again there’s no preference in which approach to choose?
Lastly, you lean towards the use of individual covariates instead of groups, since the code is more stable?

3) Using a finite mixture models, i.e. hcov=”Sex”
Those are especially useful as ‘hybrid’ models, when there are individuals of unknown sex. Since mixture models are for detection parameters only and don’t let me model different sex specific densities, they are not suitable for my question.

Independently, I will continue with discretized polygons from now on.

Many thanks,
Lukas

Any time 'secr' causes R to crash we know there's a bug. It would help me find it if you sent a (preferably simple) example - to my private email if necessary.

All available methods for sex differences in detection give the same answers (used correctly!). It's a misconception that the hybrid mixture models do not provide density estimates for each sex. derived(fit, groups = 'Sex') will do it (for conditional likelihood or full likelihood with D~1).
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I just read Durbach et al. 2024 in Biometrics (10.1093/biomtc/ujad020). They caution against using predicted AC surfaces as density surfaces. Am I wrong to feel that really, there's "nothing new here", since Murray has had that section "this is not a density surface" in the secr documentation for a long time? At least I think that's what Durbach et al. seem to argue, right? Or do I miss something big?

I'm still a bit unsure of what they're talking about, because of the differing terminology between authors and because I just came back from a very distracting vacation:

If I have a SECR model with inhomogeneous density (several spatial density covariates) and use predictDsurface() to create a map -- does that correspond to what Durbach et al. describe in section 2.1.: Expected AC density surface.

"The first we call the “expected AC density” surface. This is D(s|β), the intensity function of the underlying point process that is assumed to have generated the ACs. We use the term “expected,” because the intensity of the point process at s is approximately the expected number of ACs per unit area generated by the process in some small region surrounding s (and is exactly the expectation as the area of the region approaches 0). This quantity depends only on the parameters of the point process, and is not specific to any particular realization of points. (...)" .

I could really use some elucidation here. Thank you all.

Mirjam Barrueto,
PhD student, UCalgary

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for this comment and confirmation, Ian! These technical papers often come a bit as a shock to me, because the language between researchers, groups, Bayesian vs not, differ and it’s not always clear to me right away which concepts are actually the same. And which are new issues that I had not considered yet but should! I read your paper just as I was creating several expected AC density surfaces for a manuscript 😉.

...side note, a collaborator has been plotting multi-year time series of predicted AC location surfaces of a declining wildlife population to get a sense for where changes in our study area may be the biggest. Our thought is that if the environmental variables stay roughly the same across time in most of the study area (which we know very well), but individual distribution changes, the places where the changes are the largest may say something about underlying causes. This wouldn't necessarily be reflected in expected AC density surfaces because our data isn't high res enough to model such (localized) changes. So, I do feel that there may be valuable information contained in those predicted AC location surfaces about certain processes, just as you suggest in the paper.

Cheers,

Mirjam

Hi Mirjam,

Not adding anything Murray hasn't said, but as a co-author of that paper I thought I should say something! You're totally right - predictDsurface gives you expected AC density surfaces. It's the other surface (what we called predicted AC location surfaces / what you get from fx.total) that are often misinterpreted, though not by secr users, maybe because of the warning in the vignette.

You're also right about it not being new. We do quote the vignette, and a similar warning in the Royle et al SCR book, but since misinterpretations still happen we tried to flesh these out.

Ian
